headline: AI's Trillion-Dollar Bet, a Rainforest Ancestor and Baboon-Hunting Eagles
teaser: Is a $1.5 trillion price tag a forecast or a bubble? Could an ancient human thrive in a rainforest? And were our ancestors ever on an eagle's menu?

articles.title: Anthropic's Giant IPO Puts the AI Boom to the Test
articles.dek: A $1.5 trillion stock-market debut shows huge faith in artificial intelligence, but is the price a sound forecast or a sign that excitement is racing ahead of evidence?
paras: On Thursday, 19 November, shares of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude family of AI models, are due to begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker "ANT". The night before, the firm priced its stock at $83 a share, above the $70–$78 range it had suggested only days earlier, giving it a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion. According to reports, orders from investors were nearly seven times larger than the number of shares on offer. For a company founded only in 2021, it is an extraordinary debut, and many observers see it as a referendum on the entire artificial-intelligence boom.

An initial public offering (IPO) is the moment a private company first sells its shares to the general public. Until now, Anthropic has been owned by its founders, its employees and a relatively small circle of large investors, including technology giants such as Google and Amazon. By listing on a stock exchange, the company gains access to an enormous pool of capital, while ordinary savers gain the chance to own a slice of it. In return, Anthropic must publish detailed financial accounts every quarter and answer to thousands of shareholders who will judge its performance day by day.

The figures in the company's filings help to explain the excitement. Anthropic reported revenue of $33.2 billion for the first nine months of 2026, more than twelve times the figure for the same period a year earlier, including nearly $17 billion in the third quarter alone. The number of business customers paying it at least $100,000 a year climbed from about 950 to more than 11,900. Arun Sundararajan, a professor at New York University's Stern School of Business, has argued that there is "no real historical analogy" for a company growing at this pace. To supporters, such numbers suggest that AI has moved beyond hype and is becoming a genuine engine of economic activity.

Yet rapid growth is not the same as profit. The same filings show an operating loss of about $1.26 billion over those nine months, driven largely by the cost of computing power. Training and running advanced AI models requires vast data centres packed with expensive chips, and Anthropic has made commitments to spend close to $1 trillion on chips and infrastructure through 2045. In other words, the company is wagering that demand will keep rising fast enough to pay for capacity it is buying years in advance. If that demand slows, those commitments could become a heavy burden.

Sceptics also point to forces beyond the company's control. Rivals such as OpenAI, Google and Meta are racing to build similar systems, while cheaper open-source models could tempt customers to switch. Some politicians have begun calling for tighter rules on AI and even pauses on new data-centre construction. History offers a further warning: according to Yahoo Finance, every one of the twelve biggest US stock-market debuts since 2008 was trading below its first-day price within a year. The investor Bradley Tusk has warned that the pressure of quarterly targets could push the company to release products faster than it might otherwise choose.

That pressure matters because Anthropic has built its reputation on caution. Its founders left OpenAI partly because of concerns about AI safety, and the company has long argued that powerful systems should be developed carefully and tested thoroughly before they are released. Public markets, however, tend to reward speed and short-term results. Whether a firm can satisfy impatient shareholders while still taking its time on safety is one of the most interesting questions raised by the listing, and it is a question that may not be answered for years.

The outcome will not affect only professional traders. Up to 20 per cent of the shares have been set aside for individual investors through popular brokerage apps, and millions of people already have indirect exposure to AI through pension funds and retirement accounts that hold large technology stocks. A strong debut could lift confidence across the sector and encourage businesses to adopt AI more quickly. A weak one could suggest that investors are becoming more selective about paying premium prices for AI companies, with ripple effects far beyond a single firm.

Ultimately, an IPO price is a collective forecast rather than a final verdict. It reflects what buyers believe the company will earn many years from now, not what it earns today. Optimists see Anthropic as an early leader in a technology that could transform how people work; pessimists see a familiar pattern in which excitement races ahead of evidence, as it did during the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s. Thursday's trading will reveal the market's first opinion, but the real test of the AI boom will arrive slowly, quarter by quarter.

speak.p: Some people think teenagers should learn how the stock market works and even practise investing small amounts of money. Others think this is too risky and should wait until adulthood. Which view do you agree with, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: Choose one side; give two reasons (e.g., learning about risk early, understanding news like today's IPO) and one example; finish with a short conclusion.

write.p: Dr. Lee: This week a major artificial-intelligence company listed on the stock market at a value of about $1.5 trillion, even though it is not yet profitable. Some economists say such high prices reflect a real technological revolution; others warn of a bubble that could hurt ordinary savers. In your opinion, is the huge amount of money flowing into AI companies mostly a positive or a negative development for society? Why? Mia: "I think it is mostly positive. Investment pays for the expensive research and data centres that new technologies need. Without big investors willing to take risks, useful tools like AI tutors or medical assistants would arrive much more slowly." Ethan: "I'm more worried. When prices rise this fast, many people buy because they fear missing out, not because they understand the business. If the bubble bursts, pension funds and small investors could lose a lot, and that money could have supported other industries."
steps: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Respond to Mia or Ethan and add a new idea of your own.
Support it with one specific example, ideally from the article.
Finish with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Homo erectus Survived Longer Than Thought in China's Rainforests
articles.dek: Fossil teeth from Guangxi suggest an ancient human species lasted far longer than believed, and in a habitat many thought it could not handle. What, then, finally wiped it out?
paras: For decades, the story of Homo erectus seemed to have a clear ending. This long-legged human relative, which left Africa almost two million years ago and spread as far as Java and northern China, was thought by many researchers to have vanished from mainland Asia around 400,000 years ago. Two papers published in Nature on 18 November challenge that view. Eight fossil teeth from two caves in Guangxi, in southern China, suggest that the species survived there until somewhere between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, up to 200,000 years longer than previously believed.

Homo erectus was the first human species with body proportions similar to our own, and it was remarkably successful, surviving for well over a million years. Scientists have usually linked it with open grasslands and woodlands, where large animals could be hunted or scavenged. Tropical rainforests, by contrast, were regarded as a hostile home: food is scattered, and prey animals hide high in the canopy or move quickly through dense vegetation. This led to a widespread assumption that only Homo sapiens possessed the skills needed to live in such places.

The new teeth came from Baxian and Naxian caves, near the city of Chongzuo. Curiously, the researchers believe that porcupines collected many of the bones, since these rodents gnaw on bones to keep their teeth sharp. To identify the human teeth, the team, which included scientists from Australia, Germany and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, examined their internal shape and also extracted ancient proteins, which can survive far longer than DNA in very old fossils. Both lines of evidence pointed to Homo erectus. A ninth tooth could not be identified and may belong to a Denisovan or another archaic group.

Establishing the age of the fossils was just as important. The researchers applied five independent dating techniques to the teeth, to mineral deposits that had formed on them and to the surrounding layers of cave sediment. By combining these methods, the authors are able to describe the teeth as the youngest securely dated evidence of Homo erectus in mainland China. Using several methods matters in this field, since a single technique can be thrown off by water seeping through the rock or by material shifting between layers over thousands of years.

The second paper reconstructed the world these hominins inhabited. Chemical signals locked inside tooth enamel record what an animal ate and drank as it grew. The signals from the human teeth closely matched those of animals found in the same caves, including orangutans and an extinct forest elephant, and they pointed to diets based on dense rainforest. Strontium, an element that reflects the local rock, revealed that some individuals had moved over large areas during childhood, possibly travelling from as far away as present-day northern Vietnam.

If these interpretations are correct, a popular explanation for the species' disappearance needs rethinking. Researchers had argued that Homo erectus died out as its preferred open habitats turned into forest, because it lacked the flexibility to adapt. "They're very flexible, they're adaptable, and they're mobile," said Renaud Joannes-Boyau of Southern Cross University, one of the study's leaders. Ben Marwick of the University of Washington, who was not involved, suggested that the belief that only our species could cope with rainforests may reflect a kind of "Homo sapiens exceptionalism".

Not everyone is ready to rewrite the textbooks, however. Julien Louys of Griffith University noted that the conclusion rests on a small sample of teeth, even though he agreed that, if confirmed, the findings would show unusual ecological flexibility. Jesse Martin of La Trobe University argued that the result is less surprising than it seems, because Homo erectus persisted on the Indonesian island of Java until little more than 100,000 years ago, in a region that was itself becoming increasingly forested.

The discovery therefore raises as many questions as it answers. If Homo erectus could thrive in a rainforest refuge for so long, then a lack of adaptability may not explain why it eventually disappeared, and scientists must look harder at other factors, such as climate swings, competition or disease. Southern China, once seen as a remote corner of human prehistory, is now at the centre of that debate. As one researcher put it, the teeth "give evidence of Homo erectus surviving in rainforests", and that alone makes our ancestors' story more complicated, and more interesting, than it once appeared.

write.p: Dr. Chen: New fossil teeth from southern China suggest that Homo erectus survived in rainforests much longer than scientists believed. Discoveries like this often overturn what students learn in school. Some people say textbooks should only include ideas that are firmly established; others argue that students should learn about new, still-debated findings too. Which approach do you prefer, and why? Lucas: "I think textbooks should stick to established facts. Students have limited time, and if they learn ideas that are later rejected, they will be confused. New findings can be added once scientists agree on them." Sofia: "I disagree. Science is always changing, and this discovery shows that even "facts" can be wrong. Learning about current debates teaches students how scientists use evidence, which is more valuable than memorising conclusions."
steps: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Respond to Lucas or Sofia and add a new idea of your own.
Support it with one specific example, ideally from the article.
Finish with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Eagles Can Kill Baboons as Heavy as Early Humans
articles.dek: Skulls in the Sahara suggest eagles can kill primates far bigger than scientists believed. Were our early ancestors also on the menu, and how strong is the evidence?
paras: In 1924, workers at a quarry in South Africa uncovered the skull of a young child who had lived about 2.8 million years ago. The Taung Child, an early human relative known as Australopithecus, became one of the most famous fossils in the world. Decades later, scientists noticed small holes and scratches in its eye sockets and concluded that it had probably been killed by a large eagle. However, the child weighed only about ten kilograms. Adult hominins, it was widely assumed, were simply too heavy for birds of prey to tackle.

That assumption rested partly on a single number. Before now, no primate heavier than about 13 kilograms had ever been confirmed as the victim of a raptor. Since many early hominins weighed more than twice that much, researchers concluded that our ancestors had been largely safe from eagles for around 2.5 million years. A study published on 18 November in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology suggests that this threshold may be far too low.

The evidence comes from the Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, a rugged sandstone landscape in the Sahara that is home to an isolated population of baboons. While searching for the animals, a team led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews found skulls and bones lying at the foot of steep cliffs. "We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them," Hobaiter said. The remains told a different story.

The team examined nine baboons, eight of them adult males with an estimated average weight of about 22 kilograms; a later find weighed roughly 26 kilograms. Several skulls had deep punctures around the eye sockets, and some shoulder blades were raked with long scrapes. According to the authors, this pattern matches the lethal grip of a large eagle striking from above. The most likely culprit is the Verreaux's eagle, a bird weighing up to about seven kilograms that normally hunts much smaller prey such as rock hyraxes.

Behaviour supported the bones. When a pair of Verreaux's eagles swept overhead, the baboons gave alarm calls and dropped to safety, yet they stayed relaxed around other large raptors. Hobaiter noted that "primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat." Nathaniel Dominy of Dartmouth College, the study's senior author, admitted that the team had begun as sceptics before concluding that "the evidence was convincing."

Other experts are more cautious. No one actually saw an eagle kill a baboon, and the authors describe their findings only as "consistent with" eagle predation. Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, who studies eagles in desert environments, has questioned whether the birds attacked healthy adults at all, arguing that the baboons may already have been weak or dead and that the marks could have been made while eagles fed on carcasses. Robert Simmons of the University of Cape Town considers such attacks rare, suggesting that a shortage of prey in the desert could push eagles towards unusually large and risky targets.

Even so, the study reopens an important question about human evolution. Adult baboons of 22 to 26 kilograms are similar in size to some early hominins, and the famous skeleton Lucy is usually estimated at about 29 kilograms. If eagles can kill primates of that size today, our ancestors may have been more vulnerable than textbooks suggest. W. Scott McGraw of Ohio State University stresses that this remains a hypothesis, since no hominin fossils were examined, but it could help explain behaviours that humans share with other primates, such as warning calls and mobbing, in which adults charge together to drive an attacker away.

The authors even speculate that early hominins may have benefited from travelling in mixed groups with other primates, much as some monkeys do today in forests where eagles hunt. Such ideas are provisional, and the sample is small and comes from a single population. Yet the Ennedi bones are a useful reminder that scientific limits are sometimes built on missing evidence rather than firm proof. A threshold that stood for decades turned out to depend largely on where researchers had, and had not, looked.
